name: Liam Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Liam. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah. I'm a junior buyer at an electrical wholesaler, the kind of place electricians come to at seven in the morning for cable, switches, fuse boards and conduit. I buy the small fast-moving stuff from about forty suppliers, mostly by email and supplier portals. I've only been doing it a year, so my boss Marguerite still checks anything over five thousand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly, honestly. I've got an AI assistant that reads the supplier price lists and flags when copper cable jumps, which it does every few weeks. I'm not great at the maths of reorder points yet, so I lean on it, and sometimes it's wrong and Marguerite catches it. I like that part, figuring out where the tool is good and where it's daft.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with two mates near the ring road, rent's about a third of my pay. I've got roughly four months of costs put away. I volunteer on Saturdays at a repair café, fixing toasters and lamps, which is the most hands-on thing I do all week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype people got it wrong and the tools are still handy for the boring bits. Online I'd probably post a thread about how the gains went to shareholders anyway, even if they were small. At work I'd keep showing people the price-list trick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fine. My job sits on top of the tools, and if they stay at this level, I'm the junior who knows them best. The thing that worries me more is rent, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and push to get the price-flag setup used across the whole buying team. I'd ask Marguerite if I can take on the cable range properly, which is the hard one with copper prices. And I'd keep the four months saved, maybe nudge it to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's actually a bit of a relief to have time to get good at the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent worries you more than AI. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our landlord put it up by eight percent last spring, and he hinted at another rise. If it goes again I'd probably move further out, past the industrial estate. That's a longer bus to work, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at work struggle even in this quieter picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who does the counter, hates any screen. If the till system gets an AI upgrade he'll moan for a month. But nobody loses their job over it in this version.

say: I'd say the **hype was wrong**, but the tools still help with the boring bits.
I'd post that even **small gains** mostly went to **shareholders**, not workers.
think: My job sits **on top** of the tools, so staying at this level suits me.
**Rent rises** worry me more than AI in this picture.
do: Roll out the **price-flag setup** to the rest of the buying team.
Ask Marguerite to let me run the **cable range**, the hardest one with copper prices.
Grow savings from **four to five months** of costs.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **relieved** to have time to get good at the job.
S0.quote: My job sits on top of the tools, and if they stay at this level, I'm the junior who knows them best.
fieldNote: He treats AI as **his edge** as a junior who's still weak on reorder maths.
His real pressure is **housing costs**, and he'd move further out rather than panic.
His left-leaning view shows in who he thinks **captures the gains**.

steps.text: Get the AI price-flag setup used across the buying team
Ask to take over the copper cable range from Marguerite
Build savings from four to five months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure buyers don't just get binned. I'd be pushing online for the firms that save on staff to fund training, maybe through a levy. At work I'd volunteer to be the person who sets the new system up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of the buying team shrinks, and I'm junior, so I'm exposed. But I'm also the one already doing this with the tools. If they keep two buyers out of five, I want to be one of the two who runs the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask Marguerite for a seat on whatever group picks the new purchasing software. I'd do an online course in supply-chain data, maybe three hundred, evenings over a few months. And I'd look at jobs at the software vendors themselves, helping wholesalers set the systems up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but kind of buzzing too. It's risky, but it's the kind of change I'm built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited, but you just said the team shrinks. Who goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Joanne, who's been buying lighting for twelve years and does it all by phone. That's the bit that bugs me. I'd be fine and my colleague Joanne wouldn't, and that's not fair just because I'm younger and like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that unfairness, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the firm to keep people on while they retrain, and I'd say it to Marguerite directly. I'd also offer to sit with Joanne and show her the system. It's not much, but it's something.

say: I'd say buyers shouldn't get **binned**, and firms saving on staff should fund **training levies**.
I'd **volunteer** at work to set up the new purchasing system.
think: The **buying team shrinks**, and as a junior I'm exposed.
I want to be one of the **two buyers** who run the system when five become two.
do: Ask for a seat on the group choosing the **purchasing software**.
Take an evening **supply-chain data course**, about three hundred over a few months.
Look at jobs at **software vendors** helping wholesalers set up systems.
feel: **Uneasy**, but also **buzzing** about change he feels built for.
S1.quote: I'd be fine and my colleague Joanne wouldn't, and that's not fair just because I'm younger and like screens.
fieldNote: He expects to **land on his feet** because he already runs the tools daily.
Guilt about older colleagues like Joanne (lighting buyer) shapes his **fairness** politics.
He'd consider jumping to the **vendor side** rather than waiting.

steps.text: Join the group choosing the new purchasing software
Take an evening supply-chain data course for about three hundred
Apply for setup roles at purchasing software vendors
Campaign online for a training levy on firms that cut staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is an emergency and we need income support yesterday. I'd be at the protests, probably. At work I'd say, look, the system will do all of our jobs by 2028, so let's at least negotiate how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm out by 2028 like everyone else at a desk, maybe a few months later because I'd be the one switching things off. Being good with AI doesn't help when the AI doesn't need a minder. The electricians coming in at seven get until about 2031, which honestly makes their trade look a lot better than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrician's apprenticeship application this year, even at a pay cut, because hands-on work buys three more years. I'd cut my spending hard, drop the gym, cook in, and try to get to six months saved. And I'd join a union or a tenants' group, whatever's organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep a straight face at work but I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you're built for change. Why doesn't that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in Steady Disruption there's a gap for someone like me between the old way and the machine. With full AGI in two years, the gap closes before I can stand in it. Adaptable just means I see it coming a bit earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the electricians at the counter say to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd take the mick, probably, the buyer coming to learn wiring. But a couple of them have offered to take on an apprentice before. I'd ask Sean, he does housing estates, and he's always moaning he can't find anyone.

say: I'd call it an **emergency** that needs **income support** immediately.
I'd tell colleagues we should at least **negotiate how** the system replaces us.
think: Everyone at a desk is out by **2028**, and being good with AI doesn't save me.
Electricians get until about **2031**, so their trade beats mine.
do: Apply for an **electrician's apprenticeship** this year, even at a pay cut.
**Cut spending** hard and push savings to **six months**.
Join a **union or tenants' group** that's organising.
feel: **Alarmed**, keeping a straight face at work but lying awake running numbers.
S2.quote: Being good with AI doesn't help when the AI doesn't need a minder.
fieldNote: His **adaptability** turns into a fast switch to hands-on work, not a reason to relax.
He reads the **three-year gap** before robots as the real lifeline.
He'd ask Sean (an electrician customer) for an **apprenticeship**.

steps.text: Ask Sean for an electrician's apprenticeship this year
Drop the gym and cook in every night
Push savings from four to six months of costs
Join a union or tenants' group that's organising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's not waste it like we did with climate. I'd be online arguing for a jobs guarantee and paid retraining. At work I'd keep being the tools guy, but I'd be honest that it's temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get about four good years in buying, maybe as the person running the system. Then it's done around 2031. That's enough time to finish an apprenticeship before it lands, which wasn't true in the two-year picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the wholesaler for now and start a part-time electrical course at the college, two evenings a week. In year two I'd look for an apprenticeship that fits round it. I'd keep about five months saved so I can take the pay drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Five years means there's a ladder to climb down instead of a drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical, and not something else hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the products already, I buy them every day, and the repair café has me half-trained on wiring. It also lasts until about 2034, when the robots come. After that, I honestly don't know, nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be honest at work that it's temporary. What would you tell Marguerite?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'll set the system up properly and train the others, but I'm planning my way out. She'd get it, she's said herself she's thinking about early retirement. Better she hears it from me than finds my course timetable on the printer.

say: I'd say **five years** is a warning we mustn't waste like **climate**.
I'd argue online for a **jobs guarantee** and paid retraining.
think: I get about **four good years** in buying, maybe running the system, then it ends around **2031**.
Five years is enough to **finish an apprenticeship** before AGI lands.

Look for an **apprenticeship** in year two that fits around the course.
Keep about **five months** saved to absorb the pay drop.
feel: **Anxious**, but workable, like a ladder instead of a drop.
S3.quote: Five years means there's a ladder to climb down instead of a drop.
fieldNote: He links the **warning time** directly to whether an apprenticeship can finish.
His Saturday **repair café** gives him a head start in electrical work.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-evening part-time electrical course at the college
Argue online for a jobs guarantee and paid retraining
Keep five months of costs saved for the apprenticeship pay drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to redesign work, shorter weeks, retraining, the lot. I'd probably get involved in a local campaign group. At work I'd say this is fine, let's plan it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly relaxed. I'd have time to become a qualified electrician by thirty and then maybe move into installing solar or heat pumps, which needs people on roofs until about 2039. Ten years is half a career for someone my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for two or three years and get really good at it, especially the energy products. Then I'd start an apprenticeship, maybe through a firm I already buy from. I'd keep saving steadily and maybe put a bit into a pension instead of only cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's a long way off, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything make you less relaxed in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat. If rents keep going up and I take an apprentice wage, I'm back to sharing with three people at thirty. That's not AI, that's just how housing is, but it's the part I'd actually lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, she's been on at me to get a trade since I left school. She'll say I told you so, and she'll be right. Then probably the guys at the repair café.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a chance to **redesign work**: shorter weeks and retraining.
I'd join a **local campaign group** and tell colleagues to plan properly.
think: I can be a **qualified electrician** by thirty, then move into **solar** or heat pumps.
Ten years is **half a career** at my age, so I'm fairly relaxed.
do: Stay in buying two or three years and learn the **energy products** range.
Start an **apprenticeship** through a supplier I already buy from.
Put some savings into a **pension**, not only cash.
feel: **Uneasy** in a mild way, with **housing costs** the real worry.
S4.quote: Ten years is half a career for someone my age.
fieldNote: The long warning makes his **trade switch** comfortable rather than desperate.
His real anxiety stays with **rent**, which AI doesn't change.

steps.text: Keep buying for two or three years, focused on energy products
Start an electrical apprenticeship through a supplier he buys from
Pay part of his savings into a pension
Join a local campaign group on shorter weeks and retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even being quick doesn't help when there's no time to finish a trade. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, so you could retrain at twenty-eight without losing your flat. Some kind of rent cap too, honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who aren't on screens. Everyone talks about office jobs, but the counter staff and drivers get hit a few years later and nobody's planning for them either. That's three years of warning we keep ignoring.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about office jobs, but the counter staff and drivers get hit a few years later and nobody's planning for them either.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old junior buyer** at an electrical wholesaler, sharing a flat with two friends.
He uses **AI tools daily** and sees them as his edge while he's still weak on reorder maths.
He moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
His plan in every fast picture is an **electrician's apprenticeship**, helped by his Saturday repair café.
He worries about **older colleagues** and rent as much as about his own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there isn't time to finish a trade before desk work goes.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships** and a **rent cap** so he could retrain without losing his flat.
